header.title: Support
header.tagline: How to get help, and answers to what people ask.

help.title: Getting help
help.p2: Choose Tell us what's broken in the game's menu, or open an issue on GitHub. Issues are public.
help.p4: To report a private issue, or for anything else, email help@openhearts.game.

faq.title: Questions
faq.p2: Go to play.openhearts.game, or (coming soon) search for “Open Hearts” in the {{appStore}} or {{googlePlay}}.
faq.p6: Tap the Subscribe button under Play live. On the web, payment is on Stripe's page, and Link, Stripe's affiliate, sells the subscription. In the phone apps, it is through the App Store or Google Play, which bill and renew it. Subscribing makes your account: your name, picture, rating and games go with it onto any device you add (up to 5), and a change to your profile on one of them shows on all of them.
faq.p8: Open the menu, choose Subscription, then Manage subscription. That opens the store you subscribed in, or for the web Stripe's billing page, where you cancel; a web subscription can also be cancelled at link.com.
faq.p9: How do I add another device?
faq.p10: On a device in your account, open the menu, choose Subscription and tap Add a device, then scan the code with the other device, or tap Send the link instead. A code works once, for ten minutes.
faq.p11: What if I lose my phone, or clear my browser?
faq.p12: If another of your devices is in your account, add the new one from there and drop the lost one. If not, use a backup code: on the new device, open the menu, choose Activate subscription and enter it, and the device joins the same account, with your name, picture, rating and games. Signed in with Apple or Google? Sign in the same way on the new device instead. Any device in the account can Show backup codes, and a web subscription's were emailed when you subscribed: keep them somewhere safe. Bought in the App Store or Google Play? On the new phone, tap Subscribe, then Restore purchases.
faq.p21: Why does it say Open Hearts is open on another device?
faq.p22: Your account plays live on one device at a time, and the one opened most recently is the one in use. The other steps back: it leaves any table it was at and stops playing live, and you can still play alone on it. Tap Use it here to take the account back. If your account is in a game on the other device, you are asked first, because that game will be lost: a bot finishes your seat, and a rated game counts as one you left.
faq.p23: What if nobody else is online?
faq.p24: Ten seconds after you start waiting, bots fill the empty seats. You can play with bots at once instead, or wait up to five minutes for a person: we are told someone is waiting, and one of us may come and play. What we are told is in the privacy policy.
faq.p13: Can I play with a screen reader, or bigger text?
faq.p14: Yes. Every card, seat, trick and score has a name a screen reader can read. In a browser, press Enable accessibility, the first button a screen reader finds, and use the browser's zoom for bigger text. In the phone apps, turn on VoiceOver (iPhone) or TalkBack (Android); the app follows the phone's text size.
faq.p16: The game follows your device's language. On the web, choose another under Language on the game's About page, or with the language menu at the foot of this site. On a phone, use the phone's own setting for each app: on an iPhone, Settings, then Open Hearts, then Language; on Android 13 and later, Settings, then System, then Languages, then App languages.
faq.p17: How do I know the deal is fair?
faq.p20: Alone, nothing leaves your device. Live play shows your name, picture, account number and results publicly. Nothing is sold or used for ads. More in the privacy policy.

rules.title: What are the rules for Hearts?
rules.r2: Pass three cards: left, right, across, then no pass.
rules.r3: The two of clubs leads. Follow suit if you can.
rules.r4: No points on the first trick, unless you have nothing else.
rules.r5: Hearts can't be led until one has been played.
rules.r6: Each heart is one point; the queen of spades is thirteen.
rules.r7: Take all twenty-six to shoot the moon: everyone else gets them.
rules.r8: Play to fifty or a hundred. Lowest score wins.
rules.more: For more detail on rules and game history, see Wikipedia.

fair.random: Random. At a live table every device shuffles the deck in turn and proves it shuffled honestly, so one honest device is enough for a fair deal. Each hand opens for its own player alone: no other player sees it, and no server does. Alone, every deal comes from your device's secure random generator.
fair.witness: Witnessed. Each hand draws jurors: strangers picked at random from other players online, with no stake in the table. They play any seat a bot holds, and keep pieces of each player's keys, so a hand can finish when someone leaves while nobody alone can open another's cards. When too few other players are online to make a jury, our service's backup jurors make up the number. Like any juror, they cannot see your cards alone, only together with another player at your table, so for those hands you are trusting us not to collude.
fair.audit: Audited. After each hand every device publishes its secret, so the whole game can be replayed and every shuffle, card and play checked. After a live game, See the whole game does that check for you; after a game alone, Copy record keeps it.
fair.more: How it all works is in the write-up.

meta.title: Privacy — Open Hearts
meta.description: What Open Hearts does with your data: what stays on your device, what live play makes public, and what we keep.

header.title: Privacy
header.tagline: What Open Hearts does with what you give it, in plain words.

short.title: The short version
short.p1: Playing alone stays on your device
short.p2: Your games against the bots are kept on the device you play on, and not sent anywhere. So are your name and picture, until you subscribe: then our service keeps them with your account too, so that all its devices show the same ones.
short.p3: Live play is public, on purpose
short.p4: To play people, your name, your picture, your account's number and your results go through our relay, where anyone who asks can read them. Rooms and pictures are kept there a day; results are kept for the ratings.
short.p5: Accounts, but no email or password
short.p6: Nothing is sold, rented or used for advertising, and nothing follows you from site to site. The game on the web reports its errors and load times to New Relic, as described below; this site and the phone apps report nothing. Subscribing makes an account: a random number our service gives you, which your devices play under. There is no password, and we hold no email address.
short.p8: On the web a subscription is bought from Link, Stripe's affiliate, which has your email address, card and billing address. We keep a note of which account it pays for and which devices are in that account. We never see your card number.

who.title: Who we are
who.p1: This policy describes what Open Hearts does with data. It is not part of the terms, and it covers what they cover; "we" are who they say. The code is public, so everything on this page can be checked against what the app actually does.

device.title: On your device
device.p1: The app keeps these on the device you play on — in the browser's storage for play.openhearts.game, or in the app's own storage on a phone:
device.p2: A key your device makes for itself. It is a long random number with a public half and a secret half. The public half is this device at a live table; if you subscribe, your licence ties it to your account. The secret half never leaves the device.
device.p3: Your name and how you look: an icon and a colour, or a picture of your own. The picture is cut down to 64 by 64 pixels on your device, and only that small copy is kept. The photo you picked it from is not stored or sent. If you subscribe, our service keeps a copy with your account, as below.
device.p4: Your last thirty games against the bots, which your profile counts up. They leave the device only if you tap Copy record.
device.p5: How quickly you play, your game options, the language you chose, your licence and your account's number if you subscribe, the players whose pictures you chose to hide and those you blocked, and the notices of changes to the terms or this policy that you dismissed.
device.p6: The live game you are in, while you are in it: the table, every move and vote your device signed there, and the secrets it dealt your cards with, so that a page reloaded mid-game can come back to its seat. It is deleted when the game ends or you leave it. If the app closes mid-game, it is deleted the next time the app opens, unless that is within two minutes, when you go back to your seat.
device.p7: To remove all of it, clear the data of play.openhearts.game in your browser (and of openhearts.game, where a browser that played before the game moved to play.openhearts.game keeps its earlier copy), or delete the app. That also removes your key, so the device comes back as a new player, until a backup code or your sign-in brings it into your account again.

alone.title: Playing alone
alone.p1: A game against the bots is played entirely on your device. Nothing about it is sent anywhere.
alone.p2: The phone apps do what the game on the web does when it starts: they ask our service for the game's current settings, which says nothing about you, and make the licence check below. Live play in them works as described below. They do not use New Relic or Google's font servers.

web.title: Opening the game on the web
web.p1: Cloudflare hosts this site and the game, so it sees each request your browser makes: your IP address, your browser, and the address you asked for. We add no logging of our own.
web.p2: Google's font servers, sometimes. The game carries its own font, but when it has to draw a character that font lacks — an emoji, an arrow, or a name written in a script such as Chinese or Arabic — the toolkit it is built with fetches the extra font from fonts.gstatic.com. When that happens, Google receives your IP address and the fact that you are visiting this site.
web.p3: A licence check. Each time the game starts it sends your device's public key to our service to ask whether it holds a subscription. If it does, the service also notes that this device is the one your account is using now, when, and which live table it is at, if any; that note is replaced the next time any of your devices opens the game. If it does not, nothing is kept.
web.p4: Your profile page asks our relay for game results so it can show your rating. Nothing about you is published by it.
web.p5: New Relic tells us when the game breaks or is slow for you at play.openhearts.game. The game's page sends it the errors it meets, how long it took to load, the addresses of the calls it makes to our service (without anything after a "?"), and your browser, device type and rough location. Your IP address is used for that location and dropped within a day. It sets no cookies, records no screen or session, and reads nothing you type. Under New Relic's privacy notices.

live.title: Live play
live.p2: A live game is played between devices, through our relay, relay.openhearts.game, a server that passes messages between apps. It is open: anyone who asks it for a room, a table or the results can read what it carries there, and some of it is kept. In live play:
live.p3: Kept, and readable by anyone who asks: your name, icon and colour, your account's number, and your device's public key with the licence that ties the two together, each time you are seated at a table; your picture, if you chose one; and the result of every live game you play, rated or not — the table, each seat's account, key, licence and final score, and who left. Ratings belong to accounts and are worked out from these results by anyone who cares to, which is the point: nobody has to take our word for a rating. Names, icons, keys, account numbers and pictures are kept a day; results are kept for as long as the ratings are.
live.p4: Kept, and readable by any subscriber with the game's address: the whole of every live game once it is over — each seat's account and key, the licence tying them, the name it played under, every card dealt, passed and played, and the signatures that prove it. A player's device sends it to our service when the game ends, and it is kept for good, so a game can be looked at and checked afterwards, from the device a subscriber's account is using. Its address is a long random code that nobody can guess; it is shared by whoever shares it.
live.p5: Passed on but not kept: while you wait for a game, your name, rating, icon and colour and how many seconds you usually take over a card, every couple of seconds; and while the app is open, that your device is online or at a table, with your account's number and a short-lived note from our service saying this is the device your account is using. The relay forwards these to whoever is listening at that moment and keeps nothing — but anyone listening could record them. Reactions you send at a table (👍 Nice and the rest) are passed on the same way, to the table and anyone watching it, and not kept.
live.p6: Passed on, while anyone watches: a live game can be watched as it is played by any subscriber with its address. While someone is watching, one player's device sends, after each move, what everyone at the table can already see — the names, the scores, the cards played so far this hand and whose turn it is — and never a hand still held. The relay forwards it and keeps nothing. If you watch, it is under your own device's key and licence, so the player's device that answers sees your account's number; it answers nobody whose account is playing at that table.
live.p7: A friends' table is private in one sense only: strangers cannot sit down at it. What it publishes is as public as any other table.
live.p9: Only to our relay, which runs on Cloudflare. Every message is signed by the device that sent it, so anyone who keeps a copy can show it is genuine; we cannot delete a copy someone else made.
live.p11: The cards are dealt between the devices at the table so that each player's hand can be read by that player alone. Opening a hand would take another player at the table and a juror of the hand together, so no server of ours can read one alone. Where our service's backup jurors are on the jury, we could open a hand only together with a player at the table, and we do not. A juror holds the hand of each bot seat it plays, and the hand of a player who leaves mid-hand is opened for the rest of that hand, so that the table can finish. Plays go from device to device.
live.p12: Those connections all go through Cloudflare's relay service (TURN), so the other devices at your table never learn your IP address — not the other players, and not the jurors: the apps of other players, drawn at random, that help settle a table and play the bots' seats (or, when too few are online, our service's backup jurors). Cloudflare sees your IP address, as any server you connect to does, and passes the traffic on encrypted, so that it cannot read it.
live.p13: If nobody else is waiting and you choose to wait for a person, our service emails us that someone is waiting: the pool, the time, and the first few characters of your device's key and of your subscription — never your name or email address. One of us may come and play.
live.p14: If you report a player, our service emails us your report: what you chose and wrote, the table, the name and picture you saw, your account's number and theirs, and the first few characters of your device's key. The player isn't told. We keep a report for as long as we need it to deal with it, and our service notes for a day that you sent it, so that the same report reaches us once.

subscribing.title: Subscribing
subscribing.p1: Live play is a subscription. On the web it is bought from Link (Sold through Link, LLC), Stripe's affiliate, on Stripe's own page: it asks for your email address, your card and your billing address, which the tax where you live is worked out from, under Stripe's privacy policy.
subscribing.p2: Subscribing makes an account: a random number, not your name or email. We give Stripe your device's public key so the payment can be matched to it. In return our service keeps a short record: which account the subscription pays for, which device keys are in the account and when each was added, which one is in use now, and the dates the subscription runs to. It also keeps your account's profile — the name, icon, colour and picture you chose — so that every device in the account shows the same ones, and a change on one reaches the others. In Stripe we can see your email address, name, billing address, card brand, the last four digits of your card, and your payments and the tax on them.
subscribing.p3: That means we could connect a subscriber's email address with their account, and so with the names and results its devices have published. We do not publish that connection, and we use it only to run your subscription.
subscribing.p4: If you add another device to your account, our service keeps a record of the one-use code you made and which devices made and used it. Any device in the account can see the others' keys, which one is in use, and remove them. Your account plays on one device at a time: opening the game on one makes it the one in use, and the device before it stops playing live until you take it back.
subscribing.p5: An account also has five backup codes, kept by our service with the account and shown on its devices, with a note of which have been used. If you subscribed on the web, we write to the address you paid with in these cases only: when you subscribe, with what you bought, how it renews, how to cancel, and the codes; with the codes again, whenever a device in the account asks for them; before a change of price applies to your subscription; and when the terms or this policy change in a way that matters to subscribers, to tell you what changed. To do that we read the address from Stripe at that moment and hand it to Cloudflare, which sends the email for us; we do not keep the address, only a note of which changes your subscription was told of, and when. Link also writes to you itself about your payments, such as receipts and a reminder before each renewal, under Stripe's privacy policy.
subscribing.p6: If you sign in with Apple or Google, we keep a scrambled form of the number they give for your sign-in — not your name or email — linked to your account, so that signing in the same way on another device brings it into the account. Your device keeps only which of the two you used. Apple or Google does the signing in, under its own privacy policy; on the web, its sign-in code is fetched only while a sign-in button is on the screen.
subscribing.p7: When a subscription is bought, our service emails us which store it was bought in, the first few characters of it, and the dates it runs to, so that we can keep an eye on the service while it is small — never your name or email address.

broken.title: Telling us what's broken
broken.p1: The menu has a "Tell us what's broken" page. Nothing on it is sent until you press Send, and everything that would be sent is shown on the page first: what you write, which version of the game you have, the kind of device, the app's language and the size of the screen — and, from a game against the bots, that game's record, only if you tick the box for it. Send opens a new issue on our public GitHub page with it filled in. Anyone can read GitHub issues, so leave out anything private.

notDone.title: What we don't do
notDone.p1: No ads, and nothing sold or shared for advertising.
notDone.p2: No advertising identifiers, and nothing that follows you from app to app or site to site.
notDone.p3: No cookies from our pages. Stripe sets its own, on its own site, when you buy.
notDone.p4: No location, no contacts, no microphone. The camera only while you scan a code to add a device; the picture stays on the device.
notDone.p5: No email address held by us, no password, and no account unless you subscribe. We write to you only about a subscription, as above: nothing else, and no marketing.

kept.title: How long things are kept
kept.p1: On your device: until you remove them.
kept.p2: On our relay: moves, presence and waiting for a game: not kept. Rooms, seatings and pictures: a day. Game results: for as long as the ratings are worked out from them. A copy of each new picture, and which accounts put it out, is also kept apart for us to look at, until 30 days after it was last put out at a table, and Cloudflare, which serves that copy to us, checks it against known images of child sexual abuse. A program run by Cloudflare also looks at each new picture as it is copied, and hides one that seems to show nudity or sexual content, violence or a hate symbol; what it made of the picture is kept with the copy.
kept.p3: Finished live games: for good, in Cloudflare's storage. If you ask us to delete your account's data, your name comes off the games you played; the moves stay, for the other players.
kept.p4: Our service's account and subscription records, your account's profile among them: while the subscription runs, and afterwards until you ask us to delete them. A changed profile replaces the one before. The note of which device is in use is replaced each time another of your devices opens the game. If we suspend your account from live play, or take its name or picture off, as the terms allow, our service also keeps a note that it is suspended and since when, and the name or picture it took off, so that either can be undone. Each is kept until it is undone, or until you ask us to delete your account's records.
kept.p5: Stripe and Link: as long as Stripe's policy and the law on payment and tax records require.
kept.p6: Cloudflare and Google: under their own policies.
kept.p7: New Relic: the errors and timings, eight days.
kept.p8: What the law has us report: if something published through Open Hearts has to be reported to the authorities, as US law requires of child sexual abuse material, we keep what we reported and the account's records for as long as the law requires, a year at the least, even if you ask us to delete them, and delete them once that time is over.

choices.title: Your choices
choices.p1: Play alone, and nothing about you leaves your device.
choices.p2: Play live with a name that is not your real one, and with no picture.
choices.p3: Change your name or picture at any time; if you subscribe, the change reaches all your account's devices. What was already published stays where it is.
choices.p4: Ask us for a copy of what our service keeps about your account, its profile and its devices, or ask us to delete it. Then your name comes off the finished games you played, and the results your devices published stay on our relay, for the ratings, without your name: each still names your account's number and your device's public key. If you subscribed on the web, Stripe's payment records still hold your email address with your device's public key, which those results name, for as long as Stripe keeps them.
choices.p5: Where data protection law gives you rights — to see, correct or delete what is held about you, to object, or to complain to your data protection authority — you have them here too.

children.title: Children
children.p1: Open Hearts is not made for children under 13, and the terms do not let them play live, since it shows a name and picture to strangers. If you think a child has published something through it, tell us and we will do what we can to remove it.

changes.title: Changes
changes.p1: If what the app does with data changes, this page changes with it, and the date at the top moves. A change that matters to subscribers is told to them by email and in the app, as the terms say. Its history, and the code's, is on GitHub.

contact.title: Contact
contact.p1: For a privacy request — a copy of what our service keeps about your account, or deleting it — or any other question about this page, email help@openhearts.game, or write to us at the address in the terms. So that we can find what is yours, tell us the name you play under and, if you subscribed on the web, the email address you paid with.

header.title: Terms of Use
header.tagline: The agreement between you and Open Hearts, in plain words.

short.title: The short version
short.p2: No account, no ads, nothing to buy, and we have no plans to change that.
short.p3: Live play is a yearly subscription
short.p4: It renews automatically every year until you cancel. Cancel whenever you like, and live play lasts to the end of the year you have paid for.
short.p6: Choose a name and picture you would show anyone, and do not cheat or harass.
short.p8: It is MIT licensed. These terms are about the service we run, not about what you may do with the code.

who.title: Who these terms are with
who.p1: These terms are an agreement between you and Bright Fulton LLC, the South Carolina limited liability company that runs Open Hearts and whose address is under Contact ("Open Hearts", "we", "us"). They cover this site, the game at play.openhearts.game, the Open Hearts apps for phones, and the live-play service. By using any of them you agree to these terms. If you do not agree, please do not use them.

alone.title: Playing alone
alone.p1: Playing against the bots is free, needs no account, and has no ads or purchases in it. We do not promise to keep any particular version of it running, but the code is open, so anyone can.

subscription.title: The live-play subscription
subscription.p2: Being seated at a table with other subscribers who are waiting, with bots in the seats nobody takes.
subscription.p3: Tables of your own, with a link to send to friends who also subscribe.
subscription.p4: Rated games, and a rating worked out from results everyone at the table signs.
subscription.p5: The services that make a table work: putting devices in touch with each other, relaying the traffic between them, and jurors that keep a table going.
subscription.p6: Up to five of your devices on one subscription, added and dropped by you.
subscription.p7: Everyone at a live table has subscribed. Live play needs an internet connection; what it shares, and with whom, is in the privacy policy. We do our best to keep it working, but we cannot promise that it always will, or that a particular game will finish.
subscription.p9: A subscription lasts one year. On the web it costs {{price}} a year in US dollars, or the same in your currency at checkout, paid up front, plus any tax where you live, shown at checkout. In the App Store or Google Play the price is the one the store shows you, in your currency, before you buy.
subscription.p11: A subscription renews automatically every year, at the price then in force, and is charged to the same payment method, until you cancel it. If the price of a web subscription changes, the new price applies to yours only from a renewal we have told you of by email, at least 7 and at most 30 days before it. In the App Store or Google Play, the store tells you of a new price under its own rules.
subscription.p12: App Store: payment is charged to your Apple Account when you confirm the purchase. The subscription renews unless it is cancelled at least 24 hours before the end of the current year, and your account is charged for the renewal within the 24 hours before that.
subscription.p13: Google Play: renewal and charging follow Google Play's rules, shown when you buy.
subscription.p14: Web: you buy the subscription from Link (Sold through Link, LLC), Stripe's affiliate, which sells it for us under its purchase terms, collects any tax, and charges the payment method you gave it each year on the date you first subscribed; your card statement shows LINK.COM with our name. Before you pay, the checkout asks you to agree to these terms, and says that by subscribing you authorize Link to charge you for it until you cancel. Link sends your receipts and a reminder before each renewal, and we email you what you bought, how it renews and how to cancel. What you buy is live play, under these terms.
subscription.p16: You can cancel at any time. Cancelling stops the next renewal; live play keeps working until the end of the year you have paid for.
subscription.p17: How to cancel — in the app, in each store, and when you no longer have any of your devices — is on the support page.
subscription.p21: App Store: refunds are Apple's to give, under its own policies: ask for one at reportaproblem.apple.com. We cannot refund an App Store purchase ourselves.
subscription.p28: Google Play: ask Google, under its policies, or contact us: we can refund a Google Play purchase ourselves.
subscription.p22: Web: contact us, or Link. If you live in the EU or the UK, you may cancel the purchase within 14 days of it, under Link's purchase terms. Anywhere, a right the law where you live gives you to withdraw from the purchase or to a refund is yours, and we will look fairly at any other request.
subscription.p23: A refund ends the subscription, whoever gives it, Link included: it is not renewed again, and live play on its devices stops at the end of the day it ends (in UTC). For a purchase in a store, that is the day the store tells us of the refund.
subscription.p25: Subscribing makes an account, and the subscription and its devices belong to it. There is no password, and the account plays live on one device at a time: opening the game on another of its devices moves live play there, and a game left on the first counts as one you left. If you clear the game's data or delete the app on your only device in the account, bring the new one in with a backup code, or, if you signed in with Apple or Google, by signing in the same way again. Or contact us with the email address you paid with on the web, and we will help where we can. You are responsible for the devices you bring into your account and for what is done in live play from them, so bring in only your own, and drop one you no longer have.
subscription.p27: While the game is open on the device your account plays live on, that device may be drawn as a juror at other subscribers' tables, a hand at a time: it helps deal the cards, plays the seats the bots hold, and settles turns the players cannot. That is how live tables work without a server of ours dealing the cards, and every subscriber's device does its part. It uses some of the device's data, battery and processing while the game is open, and the device is not drawn while the game is in the background or once it is closed. What it shares, and with whom, is in the privacy policy.

table.title: At a live table
table.p1: Your name and picture are public at a live table, as the privacy policy sets out. Do not put anything in them that you would not want a stranger to see.
table.p3: use a name or picture that is hateful, sexual, violent, harassing or illegal, or that infringes someone else's rights;
table.p4: pretend to be another person, or to be us;
table.p5: harass, threaten or abuse other players;
table.p6: cheat: share cards with another player, play several seats at one table, or alter the game to gain an advantage;
table.p7: attack, overload or try to break the service, the relays or other players' devices, or abuse them, for example by flooding them or by using them to carry or store anything but the game's own traffic.
table.p10: Reading what the relay publishes and working out ratings from it are welcome, and so is looking for security problems in good faith and reporting them as our security policy asks.
table.p8: A player who stops playing can be booted by the table, and a bot takes the seat. A player who leaves a rated game finishes it last. You can hide another player's picture on your own device at any time, or block them: then their name, picture and reactions are not shown on your device.
table.p9: To report a player or a picture, hold their name at the table and choose Report, or contact us (below). Pictures are also checked automatically as they are published, and one that seems to break these rules is hidden at once; if you think yours was hidden by mistake, contact us. If a device or an account breaks these rules, we may remove its name or picture, suspend it from live play at once, and stop issuing its devices the licences live play needs. A suspended account's web subscription does not renew while the suspension lasts. If we suspend an account without a good reason, we will refund the unused part of a web subscription. We may also end an account, as Ending these terms says.

content.title: What you publish
content.p1: Your name, icon, colour and picture, and the records and results of the games you play, are yours. So that live play can work, you give us a worldwide, non-exclusive, royalty-free licence to store, copy, publish and pass them on through our service and relay, and to show them to other players and to anyone who reads the relay, as the privacy policy describes, for as long as it says they are kept. ending.p1: You can stop using Open Hearts at any time, and cancel a subscription as described above.
